Large Language Models for Bioinformatics 2026 Faculty: Hosna Jabbari, Mark Berjanskii November 14-15, 2026 Workshop Info Welcome to the 2026 Large Language Models for Bioinformatics Canadian Bioinformatics Workshop webpage! Workshop code: LLM_Ed-2611 Dates: Saturday–Sunday, November 14–15, 2026 Location: Donadeo Innovation Centre for Engineering (ICE), University of Alberta, Edmonton (in person) Workshop listing: bioinformatics.ca Travel and venue: Map, transit, and hotel information is available on the Edmonton logistics page. Weekend building-access details will be emailed closer to the workshop. About the Workshop This two-day workshop focuses on the applications of large language models (LLMs) in bioinformatics. Participants will first be introduced to foundational machine learning (ML) concepts, followed by an in-depth exploration of LLMs and their growing role in bioinformatics. The program includes lectures and hands-on labs covering LLM applications in genomics, proteomics, and natural language processing (NLP). Participants will learn how to use LLMs, and which LLMs to use, for coding in bioinformatics, gene prediction/annotation, protein structure/function analysis, and large-scale literature analysis in their research. Course Objectives After the course, participants should be able to: Explain the key concepts of large language models and their applications in bioinformatics, including genomics, proteomics, and general informatics. Apply LLMs to perform bioinformatics coding tasks. Utilize LLM-based tools for analyzing bioinformatics data in genomics, including gene prediction/annotation, protein structure/function prediction, and large-scale literature analysis. Integrate LLMs into bioinformatics workflows for research and analysis. Target Audience Post-doctoral fellows, graduate students, bioinformaticians, computational biologists, and researchers in the life sciences domain, focused on individuals involved in bioinformatics projects with an interest in applying large language models and artificial intelligence to genomics, proteomics, and NLP research. Prerequisites Participants should have a basic understanding of bioinformatics and molecular biology. Familiarity with Python programming and command-line tools is required. Some prior exposure to LLM concepts and tools would be beneficial, though not mandatory. Pre-work Please complete the two forms below before the workshop. Instructors Hosna Jabbari Photo: University of Alberta Faculty of Engineering. Engineering Research Chair in Computational Biology University of Alberta Edmonton, Alberta Dr. Hosna Jabbari is a computational biologist and Engineering Research Chair in Computational Biology at the University of Alberta. She leads the COBRA Lab, where her group studies RNA structure and function using bioinformatics, machine learning, and data science. Mark Berjanskii Research Associate University of Alberta Edmonton, Alberta Dr. Mark Berjanskii earned a PhD in Biochemistry from the University of Missouri–Columbia in 2002, studying oncoviral protein structure and dynamics with NMR. After postdoctoral research in protein structural biology at the University of Michigan, he joined David Wishart’s group at the University of Alberta to work on metabolomics, NMR, and protein structure. Teaching Assistants Amirali Loghmani Teaching Assistant University of Alberta Edmonton, Alberta Amirali Loghmani is an MSc student in Biomedical Engineering at the University of Alberta. His research uses deep learning to study SARS-CoV-2 mutations and potential variants of concern. Utkarsh Kalra Teaching Assistant University of Alberta Edmonton, Alberta Utkarsh Kalra is an MSc student in Biomedical Engineering and a Graduate Research Assistant in the COBRA Lab. His work includes machine-learning models of protein–RNA binding and analysis of single-cell genomic data.
